label: Tuesday, September 29, 2026
editor_note: Three threads run through these stories: the memory bandwidth wall behind long-context LLM inference, tiny classification models replacing general LLMs in pipelines, and latency cuts from synthesis and extreme quantization.

sections.name: engineering
sections.label: Engineering
sections.intro: A small calibrated classifier measured on consumer GPU, prompt patterns for AI-driven Android audits, and routing LLMs through specialized classification models.

stories.title: Small Decisions: Engineering a Leading Model
stories.summary: Marc Brooker built a 2B-parameter classifier by stripping the text-generation head from Qwen3.5-2B and adding a small pointer head fine-tuned with rank-16 LoRA. Inference runs in one or two forward passes regardless of question count, hitting p50 100ms and p95 under 300ms on a 3090. Per-question-type temperature scaling yields a 0.009 Brier score on easy tasks, beating Qwen3.5-2B on accuracy and calibration.
stories.why: Concrete systems-level walkthrough of building a small calibrated classifier with constant-time inference and measured latency on consumer GPU.
stories.takeaway: Replacing the text-generation head with a small pointer head turns an LLM into a calibrated classifier with constant-cost inference.

stories.title: How we found 24 Android vulnerabilities using our open source AI security agent
stories.summary: GitHub Security Lab's open-source taskflow agent used guided LLM prompts to find 24 Android vulnerabilities including OsmAnd location tracking and Wikipedia account takeover. The approach splits audit work into incremental taskflows combining strict and broad prompts across multiple runs. LLMs find bugs well but misjudge severity, so human review remains essential.
stories.why: Shows practical prompt-engineering patterns for guiding LLMs through structured code security audits.
stories.takeaway: For LLM code analysis, split audits into incremental taskflows combining strict and broad prompts, then have humans review for severity.

stories.title: Jev introduces a new shape of LLM - System One, aka Decision Models
stories.summary: Jev is a decision model: text in, typed probabilistic scores out. It charges only input tokens at $0.042 per million, cheaper than GPT-5 Nano, and evaluates questions in parallel. Useful for classification, spam, prioritization, and BM25 reranking, but it is opaque and raises bias concerns since no reasoning is returned.
stories.why: A specialized, cheap classification-only model changes how you architect LLM pipelines for routing, ranking, and labeling.
stories.takeaway: Consider replacing expensive generative LLM calls with cheap decision-model scores wherever you only need classification or ranking.

sections.name: papers
sections.label: Papers
sections.intro: KV cache memory bandwidth as the new bottleneck in long-context inference, and consensus protocols synthesized to match a given topology and workload.

stories.title: The KV Cache Is the New Memory Wall
stories.summary: At 128k tokens, a Llama-3-70B sequence's KV cache (42 GB) approaches its weight footprint (140 GB), shifting the bottleneck from weights to attention state. The paper derives closed-form bandwidth models for H100, B200, and MI300X predicting where KV traffic overtakes weight traffic, then evaluates five optimization categories under one protocol.
stories.why: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by KV cache memory bandwidth, not compute, and this paper gives the analytical framework to reason about it.
stories.takeaway: KV optimization only helps beyond a hardware-specific crossover; below it you trade complexity for no speedup.

stories.title: KCensus: Synthesizing Latency-Optimal Consensus Fast Paths (Extended Version)
stories.summary: Most fast-path consensus schemes are hand-tuned for specific conditions. The authors model fast paths as mechanisms that spread knowledge about proposals, derive a condition those mechanisms must satisfy, and turn it into an optimization problem. Their framework KCensus synthesizes optimal fast paths; a geo-replicated key-value store using it achieves up to 16% lower average latency across AWS regions.
stories.why: Cuts consensus latency by synthesizing protocols tailored to your topology and workload.
stories.takeaway: Frame consensus fast paths as knowledge-spreading to find the best one for your setting.

sections.name: tools
sections.label: Tools
sections.intro: Tiny local decision models returning probabilities in about 30 milliseconds, and a 0.5B language model distributed across seven microcontrollers running 1.58-bit weights.

stories.title: Jeff – Jev-compatible 0.8B decision models, trained at home, ~30 ms
stories.summary: Jeff fine-tunes 0.8B-2B Qwen and Gemma models for zero-shot option classification, returning calibrated probabilities in one forward pass with no text generation. Latency: 22 ms on RTX PRO 6000, 28 ms on M4 Max MLX; 0.8B trains in ~2 hours on one GPU. Overall benchmark scores approach Jev, though reasoning benchmarks lag; a domain fine-tune on ~11k examples pushed accuracy from 31.7% to 95.8%.
stories.why: Tiny local classifiers returning calibrated probabilities in ~25 ms, fine-tunable on one workstation GPU.
stories.takeaway: For routing or intent classification at scale, a small local fine-tune can beat waiting on a large remote model.

stories.title: ESP32S3 cluster running 1.58-bit (BitNet) Language model
stories.summary: A 0.5B BitNet model with 1.58-bit ternary weights is split across 7 ESP32S3 boards: a master runs BPE tokenization and INT4 embeddings, while 6 compute nodes each handle 4 transformer blocks. Hidden states pass between boards via high-speed SPI daisy-chain, with assembly-optimized MAC operations, FP16 scaled computations, and a PSRAM-backed KV cache.
stories.why: A 0.5B language model running across seven $2 microcontrollers demonstrates extreme pipeline parallelism and custom quantization in a tight distributed system.
stories.takeaway: Pipeline parallelism plus aggressive 1.58-bit quantization can make a functional LLM inference engine out of cheap microcontrollers.

sections.name: discussions
sections.label: Discussions
sections.intro: Lisp's cognitive load gets a perceptual explanation, and a short argument for keeping Go import paths independent of any single git host.

stories.title: What makes Lisp difficult to read?
stories.summary: Lisp puts the function name between opening and closing parentheses, increasing delimiter distance. This violates Gestalt laws of proximity and closure, making parens harder to match visually. C-style notation clusters delimiters tightly and benefits from working memory limits of about four items.
stories.why: Cognitive science explanation for why Lisp notation strains visual parsing, relevant to language and DSL design.
stories.takeaway: Tightly clustered delimiters match better with human visual grouping than widely-separated ones.
stories.debate: Commenters argue nested calls are inherently hard to read in any language, and Lisp's perceived difficulty is largely a familiarity issue rather than a notation problem.

stories.title: Don't couple your Go code to GitHub
stories.summary: Go's module system uses the git hosting URL as the package namespace, so moving from GitHub to GitLab forces import path changes across your codebase. Using a custom vanity domain like go.uber.org lets you redirect imports to any git host behind the scenes without changing consumer code.
stories.why: Avoids lock-in to a specific git host by keeping Go import paths independent of where code is hosted.
stories.takeaway: Set up a custom domain for Go imports to decouple your code from any single git hosting provider.
stories.debate: Commenters warn that vanity domains introduce trust risks since a domain could serve different code to the browser than to the Go toolchain, unlike a direct github.com URL.
